How to write an intensity or cumulative intensity function for vectorized models

TA Trikalinos

2026-08-28

Source: vignettes/Writing_intensity_functions.Rmd
Writing_intensity_functions.Rmd

What this vignette shows

The vectorized samplers take user functions in two roles: an intensity lambda for the thinning samplers (vdraw_intensity(), vdraw_intensity_step()), and a cumulative intensity pair Lambda / Lambda_inv for the inversion sampler (vdraw_cumulative_intensity()). This vignette states the calling contract these functions must satisfy, shows the canonical way to pass parameters – including parameters that differ across the simulated point processes – and collects the idioms and anti-patterns.

The calling contract

Every user function is called elementwise-vectorized: it receives an array of time points (or of Λ\Lambda-values, for Lambda_inv) and must return an object of the same shape, computed element by element. The samplers call

  • lambda(t) or lambda(t, a),
  • Lambda(t) or Lambda(t, a), and Lambda_inv(z) or Lambda_inv(z, a),

where a is the argument container you supplied (next section), passed as the second positional argument; the name of the second formal is yours to choose. When you supply no container the function is called with a single argument, so a plain closure works:

l <- function(t) 0.5 * sqrt(t)
Z <- vdraw_intensity(
  lambda = l,
  lambda_maj_matrix = matrix(1.2, nrow = 100, ncol = 5),
  rate_matrix_t_min = 1, rate_matrix_t_max = 5
)

The shape of the first argument depends on the sampler: the thinning samplers pass a matrix of candidate times with one row per point process; the inversion sampler passes a two-column matrix of interval bounds to Lambda and a matrix of Λ\Lambda-values to Lambda_inv (also one row per process). Elementwise arithmetic preserves shape automatically, so you rarely need to think about it – but it matters for how per-process parameters align, below.

Passing parameters: the structured container

All of the function’s parameters live in one container with two channels (slots):

lambda_args = list(
  shared   = list(...), # row-invariant parameters, any type; stored ONCE
  row_args = data.frame(...) # one row per point process
)
  • shared holds anything that is the same for every point process: scalars, vectors, matrices, spline bases, fitted model objects. It is never replicated across processes, so a large shared object costs its size once – not once per process.
  • row_args holds parameters that vary by point process: a data.frame (or data.table – accepted as-is, read-only, never coerced or copied) with one row per point process, in the same order as the rows of the rate or majorizer matrix. The samplers validate the row count.

Inside your function, access both channels through the second argument:

l <- function(t, a) {
  a$shared$scale * t^a$row_args$exponent
}
n <- 1000
args <- list(
  shared = list(scale = 0.2),
  row_args = data.frame(exponent = seq(0.5, 1.5, length.out = n))
)
Z <- vdraw_intensity(
  lambda = l, lambda_args = args,
  lambda_maj_matrix = matrix(3, nrow = n, ncol = 5),
  rate_matrix_t_min = 1, rate_matrix_t_max = 5
)

Why this aligns. t arrives as an n x M matrix and a$row_args$exponent is a length-n vector. R recycles vectors down the columns of a matrix, and the matrix has one row per process – so t^a$row_args$exponent raises every entry of row ii to exponent[i]. This column-major recycling is the relied-upon R idiom: write the function as if t were a column of times for all processes at once, index nothing by hand.

Rejection resampling is handled for you. The conditioned thinning samplers redraw only the point processes that failed the condition. In those rounds your function receives a with row_args already subset to the processes being redrawn, still aligned row-for-row with the candidate matrix. Do not cache row indices between calls.

Cumulative intensity pairs

Lambda must be continuous and increasing in t for each process, and Lambda_inv must be its inverse. One container serves both functions – there is a single Lambda_args, delivered to Lambda and Lambda_inv alike, so write the pair against the same parameterization:

L <- function(t, a) (a$shared$r + a$row_args$d) * t
Li <- function(z, a) z / (a$shared$r + a$row_args$d)
n <- 1000
ctr <- list(
  shared = list(r = 0.4),
  row_args = data.frame(d = runif(n, 0, 0.4))
)
Z <- vdraw_cumulative_intensity(
  Lambda = L, Lambda_inv = Li,
  t_min = rep(0, n), t_max = rep(10, n),
  Lambda_args = ctr
)

Two additional requirements:

  • NA in, NA out. The sampler calls Lambda_inv on NA-padded matrices (padding marks processes that have run out of events). Plain arithmetic propagates NA automatically; only special-case code (if (z > ...), table lookups) needs care – use vectorized constructs (ifelse(), pmin()/pmax(), approxfun(..., rule = 2)).
  • With output = "long" on the conditioned path, Lambda_inv receives the event vector rather than a matrix, with row_args subset to one row per event. The same elementwise code covers both cases without change.

Majorizers from the same function

get_step_majorizer() accepts the same container through fun_args, so the sampler’s lambda doubles as the input for majorizer construction – no hand-written wrapper:

l <- function(t, a) a$shared$scale * t^a$row_args$exponent
n <- 1000
args <- list(
  shared = list(scale = 0.2),
  row_args = data.frame(exponent = seq(0.5, 1.5, length.out = n))
)
breaks_mat <- matrix(rep(seq(1, 5, length.out = 6), each = n), nrow = n)
lmaj <- get_step_majorizer(
  fun = l, breaks = breaks_mat, is_monotone = TRUE, fun_args = args
)
Z <- vdraw_intensity(
  lambda = l, lambda_args = args, lambda_maj_matrix = lmaj,
  rate_matrix_t_min = 1, rate_matrix_t_max = 5
)

If lambda ever exceeds the majorizer, the kernels stop with a “Majorizer” error rather than silently sampling the wrong process – prefer a slightly generous majorizer over a tight one you have not verified.

A complete example: heterogeneous population, both algorithms

A population where each person carries a frailty and a shape parameter, and the same model is sampled by thinning (only lambda known) and by inversion (closed-form Lambda and inverse): λi(t)=witpi\lambda_i(t) = w_i \, t^{p_i}, so Λi(t)=witpi+1/(pi+1)\Lambda_i(t) = w_i \, t^{p_i + 1} / (p_i + 1).

n <- 2000
pop <- data.frame(
  w = rgamma(n, shape = 4, rate = 4), # frailty, mean 1
  p = runif(n, 0.5, 1.5)
)
args <- list(row_args = pop) # no shared channel needed; that is fine

l <- function(t, a) a$row_args$w * t^a$row_args$p
L <- function(t, a) a$row_args$w * t^(a$row_args$p + 1) / (a$row_args$p + 1)
Li <- function(z, a) (z * (a$row_args$p + 1) / a$row_args$w)^(1 / (a$row_args$p + 1))

breaks_mat <- matrix(rep(seq(0, 3, length.out = 7), each = n), nrow = n)
Z_thin <- vdraw_intensity(
  lambda = l, lambda_args = args,
  lambda_maj_matrix = get_step_majorizer(
    fun = l, breaks = breaks_mat, is_monotone = TRUE, fun_args = args
  ),
  rate_matrix_t_min = 0, rate_matrix_t_max = 3
)
Z_inv <- vdraw_cumulative_intensity(
  Lambda = L, Lambda_inv = Li,
  t_min = rep(0, n), t_max = rep(3, n),
  Lambda_args = args
)

# the two exact algorithms sample the same process
suppressWarnings(stats::ks.test(
  as.vector(Z_thin[!is.na(Z_thin)]),
  as.vector(Z_inv[!is.na(Z_inv)])
))$p.value
#> [1] 0.6577164

Anti-patterns

  • Do not replicate row-invariant parameters into row_args (row_args = data.frame(scale = rep(0.2, n))): it works, but costs n copies of what shared stores once. At 10610^6–10710^7 processes this is real memory.
  • Do not rely on the deprecated conventions: a flat lambda_args = list(...) (all-shared, kept working for released code), the nested vector_arguments element, and the separate Lambda_inv_args all emit deprecation warnings and will eventually be removed. New code uses shared/row_args and one Lambda_args for the pair.
  • Do not write functions that expect the container by name (function(t, lambda_args) called as lambda(t, lambda_args = ...)): the delivery is positional; name the second formal whatever you like, but do not depend on the name.
  • Do not modify a inside the function (in particular, no data.table by-reference operations on a$row_args): the container is read-only shared state; mutating it corrupts subsequent calls, including the resampling rounds of the conditioned thinning samplers.
  • Do not branch on scalar tests (if (t < 1) ...) – t is a matrix; use vectorized alternatives.
